section_summary: This section combines Occupation-era reports on Japanese public opinion, election polling, and political affairs. It includes a survey dominated by repatriation requests, a conversation with Japanese cabinet leaders, and a lengthy assessment of local election polls. The later documents concern Japan’s economy, Christian peace discussions, a British observer’s account of postwar society, and disagreement over the zaibatsu deconcentration program.

subfiles.title: Survey of Opinions and Attitudes Expressed in Letters by Japanese to Occupation Authorities: Report No. 15
subfiles.from: Public Opinion and Sociological Research, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Tabulates opinions and requests in Japanese correspondence received by Occupation authorities from June 1 to July 15, 1947.
subfiles.summary: Of 35,102 recorded opinions and requests, 98.4 percent concerned repatriation. The report cautions that self-selected letters and apparent writing campaigns cannot represent Japanese public opinion.

subfiles.summary: Replaces an original action copy not returned to Central Records.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1384: Memorandum of Conversation with the Chief Cabinet Secretary and the Speaker
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a November 5 conversation with Nishio and Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Cover despatch listing the conversation’s subjects, including the peace treaty, Hirano’s dismissal, communism, the Coal Bill, and the constitution.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Suehiro Nishio and Komakichi Matsuoka
subfiles.about: Records a luncheon discussion of Japanese politics and Occupation policy.
subfiles.summary: Nishio discusses peace treaty representation, Hirano’s replacement, and the constitution; Matsuoka discusses communist activity and the Coal Bill. Both seek greater continuity among Occupation personnel.

subfiles.title: Second copy of despatch 1384
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Duplicates the cover despatch forwarding the Nishio–Matsuoka conversation.

subfiles.title: Second copy of the Nishio–Matsuoka memorandum of conversation
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum of the November 5 luncheon conversation.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the discussion of peace treaty representation, Cabinet succession, communist activity, the Coal Bill, the constitution, and Occupation staffing.

subfiles.title: Telegram 470 from Seoul on Syngman Rhee’s election plans
subfiles.from: U.S. command in Korea, for Jacobs
subfiles.about: Reports intercepted Rhee telegrams concerning South Korean elections and Chinese policy at the United Nations.
subfiles.summary: The sender argues that Rhee seeks an early election to create an interim government he could dominate. The telegram quotes Rhee’s messages to Louise Yim and Chiang Kai-shek.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1403: Pre-election studies by Japanese public opinion organizations
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a Civil Information and Education Section assessment of Japanese election polls.
subfiles.summary: Transmits five copies of the October 22 report.

subfiles.title: An Evaluation of Some Pre-Election Studies by Public Opinion Organizations
subfiles.from: Public Opinion and Sociological Research, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese organizations’ predictions of 1947 local elections.
subfiles.summary: The report examines Tokyo and Kyoto mayoral polls and gubernatorial or mayoral polls in Saitama, Kumamoto, and Osaka. It credits improved interviewing, sampling, and turnout methods for more accurate predictions than in 1946, while identifying small samples, ambiguous questions, and weak turnout estimates. Across most polls, conservative support rises with age and is generally stronger among women; the political effect of nonvoting remains uncertain.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note concerning Bogdan’s report
subfiles.about: Appears to route or comment on Bogdan’s report; much of the handwriting is illegible in the OCR.
subfiles.summary: Brief, largely illegible note associated with the Bogdan memorandum.

subfiles.title: Lyon’s note to Allison on Bogdan’s Japan memorandum
subfiles.about: Requests Allison’s opinion of Bogdan’s optimistic report on Japan and the zaibatsu issue.
subfiles.summary: Lyon asks for an assessment before replying to Bogdan.

subfiles.title: Slattery’s letter forwarding Bogdan’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards Norbert Bogdan’s informal memorandum on conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Slattery encloses Bogdan’s memorandum following his visit to Japan.

subfiles.title: Lyon’s acknowledgment of Bogdan’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Thanks Slattery and Bogdan for the memorandum on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Says the report, especially its economic observations, was valuable to Department officers.

subfiles.title: Despatch 1419: Round-table Conferences on Questions Pertaining to Culture and Peace
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Christian-sponsored round-table meetings at the Japanese prime minister’s residence.
subfiles.summary: Sebald describes discussions of peace, culture, reform, education, and evangelism attended by legislators, missionaries, and Japanese ministers. He lists translated minutes and invitations as enclosures, though they do not appear in these pages.

subfiles.title: Despatch 2725: Transmitting Spectator article on Japan
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Forwards Russell Greenwood’s article, “What Japan Is Thinking.”
subfiles.summary: Lists Greenwood’s observations on recovery, religion, democracy, communism, and British cultural ties.

subfiles.title: What Japan Is Thinking
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese daily life and political attitudes under Allied Occupation.
subfiles.summary: Greenwood portrays a population focused on food and rebuilding, disillusioned with the wartime regime, and only gradually learning democratic practice. He discusses religion, the 1947 elections, limited communist gains, American dominance, and interest in closer cultural relations with Britain.

subfiles.title: Elimination of Excessive Concentrations of Economic Power in Japan (Zaibatsu Program)
subfiles.about: Recommends a State Department response to the Army’s proposed cable on Japan’s deconcentration ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Wisner supports selected Army amendments but argues that others would weaken the ordinance and prejudge a broader policy review. He distinguishes corporate reorganization from seizure of zaibatsu individuals’ assets, rejects an added requirement to prove adverse price effects, and objects to detailed Washington control over SCAP’s implementation.
